table.text: Undergraduate students (M age = 19.16 years, SD = 1.05; 81% women) were randomized to eight days of online Stoic training or an active control involving literary-fiction readings.
Ninety-eight participants completed pretraining and posttraining self-report assessments (Stoic training, n = 46; control, n = 52).
Participants were 98 undergraduate students recruited via the Hamilton College online recruitment system.
As compensation, participants were offered extra credit in their eligible psychology and neuroscience courses.

Participants were selected based on their scores on the Brief Resilience Scale (BRS; Smith et al. 2008), with applicants scoring greater than 4.3 out of 5 being excluded in order to decrease the likelihood of a ceiling effect.
table.formatted: Participants were selected based on their scores on the Brief Resilience Scale (BRS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Smith et al. 2008)</ref>, with applicants scoring greater than 4.3 out of 5 being excluded in order to decrease the likelihood of a ceiling effect.

table.text: Participants were randomly allocated to either Stoic Training (pre-training n = 61, post-training n = 46) or Active Control (pre-training n = 60, post-training n = 52).
Participants were not informed that the study involved multiple experimental conditions or that they were receiving an intervention.
After completing the training period, participants completed the same self-report questionnaires administered at baseline.
Participants were then invited to schedule a laboratory visit and were encouraged to attend within four calendar days of completing their assigned training or control activities.
Prior to the lab visit, participants were asked to refrain from caffeine for 6 hours, alcohol for 12 hours, and food and vigorous exercise for 3 hours.
During the lab visit, participants completed brief pre-task questionnaires to measure adherence to protocol and baseline state anxiety.
After completing self-report forms, participants were connected to physiological recording equipment, completed a modified TSST, and self-reported post-TSST state anxiety.
Participants were instructed to complete the eight sessions within 12 days, although additional time was permitted when necessary.

Participants completed the Stoic Attitudes and Behaviours Scale to measure Stoicism as a life philosophy (SABS; LeBon et al., 2026), Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation Scale to measure fear of negative evaluation (BFNE; Leary 1983), the Ruminative Response Scale-10 to measure rumination (RRS-10; Treynor et al., 2003), the General Self-Efficacy Scale to measure selfefficacy (GSE; Schwarzer & Jerusalem 1995), the Brief Resilience Scale to measure resilience as the ability to bounce back from stress (BRS; Smith et al. 2008), and the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale-10 to measure resilience as perceived ability to cope with and adapt to adversity (CD-RISC-10; Campbell-Sills and Stein 2007).
table.formatted: Participants completed the Stoic Attitudes and Behaviours Scale to measure Stoicism as a life philosophy (SABS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">LeBon et al., 2026)</ref>, Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation Scale to measure fear of negative evaluation (BFNE; Leary 1983), the Ruminative Response Scale-10 to measure rumination <ref type="bibr">(RRS-10;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Treynor et al., 2003)</ref>, the General Self-Efficacy Scale to measure selfefficacy (GSE; <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Schwarzer & Jerusalem 1995)</ref>, the Brief Resilience Scale to measure resilience as the ability to bounce back from stress (BRS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Smith et al. 2008)</ref>, and the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale-10 to measure resilience as perceived ability to cope with and adapt to adversity (CD-RISC-10; <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Campbell-Sills and Stein 2007)</ref>.

table.text: Participants completed a modified version of the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST; Kirschbaum et al., 1993), a standardized laboratory stressor designed to elicit social-evaluative threat.
table.formatted: Participants completed a modified version of the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST; <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Kirschbaum et al., 1993)</ref>, a standardized laboratory stressor designed to elicit social-evaluative threat.

table.text: During this phase, participants assigned to Stoic training were instructed to apply the practice of Negative Visualization to the upcoming social stress task during a 5-minute period, whereas participants assigned to the control condition were instructed to wait quietly for 5 minutes.
For the speech task, participants were instructed to give a speech about why they were qualified for their dream job in front of two evaluative panelists.
For the mental arithmetic task, participants were instructed to serially subtract 13 from 1,022 as quickly and accurately as possible and to start over if they made an error.

However, for GSR, frequent electrode detachment resulted in unreliable signal quality, and no standardized procedure was available to determine consistently which participants had provided usable recordings.

Participants were encouraged to attend the laboratory visit within four calendar days of completing their assigned training or control activities, although later visits were permitted when scheduling within this window was not feasible.

After adjustment for baseline SUDS, participants assigned to Stoic training reported numerically higher SUDS during the TSST, but the condition effect was not statistically significant, b = 3.77, SE = 3.56, t(76) = 1.06, p = .293, 95% CI [-3.33, 10.87], adjusted d = 0.24.

Contrary to prediction, participants assigned to Stoic training exhibited higher baseline-adjusted HR during the TSST and lower baseline-adjusted HRV, although the preregistered HRV effect narrowly missed the conventional significance threshold.

Participants in the Stoic condition had completed eight sessions of internet-delivered Stoic training and then engaged in five minutes of Negative Visualization immediately before receiving the speech instructions, whereas control participants completed eight sessions of the active control and spent the corresponding five-minute period waiting quietly.
All participants had complete item-level data for the measures shown.
All participants had complete item-level data for the subscales shown.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: The effects of Stoic Training on Stress Reactivity
table.research_questions:
RQ1) Does STAR bolster resilience to social stress?
H1a – Those allocated to receive STAR training will record lower sympathetic nervous system responsivity (as measured by average heart rates, skin conductance and blood pressure) during the social stress test as compared to the control group.
H1b - Those allocated to receive STAR training will record higher parasympathetic nervous system activity (as measured by average heart rate variability) during the social stress test as compared to the control group.
H1c - Those allocated to receive STAR training will record lower subjective units of distress and lower state anxiety (as measured by the STAI) as compared the control group. 
H1d – Those allocated to receive STAR training will record significant reductions in the fear of negative evaluation (as measured by the BFNE). 

RQ2) Does STAR improve resilience and decrease rumination in daily life 
H2a – Those allocated to receive STAR training will record significant reductions in rumination (as measured by the RRS-10).
H2b - Those allocated to receive STAR training will record significant increases in self-efficacy (as measured by the GSE).
H2c - Those allocated to receive STAR training will record significant increases in resilience (as measured by the BRS and CDRISC-10).
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview: This study is a two-armed randomised controlled trial, with one grouping variable (intervention), with time as a repeated measure.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures:
Participants will be recruited through Hamilton College’s research participation program (SONA) and offered course credit for their participation.

Participants will complete all measures at baseline, followed by a 12-day training period during which participants are instructed to complete 8 sessions of their assigned training (STAR or active control), after which they will complete self-report measures again.

Participants will be invited to the lab to complete physio measures and the TSST within 4 days of the completion of their training period.
table.sample_size_rationale: This is primarily based on time and resource constraints
table.manipulated_variables:
Participants will be randomly allocated to receive either:
Stoic Training for Achieving Resilience (STAR) - this consists of 8 training sessions presenting a series of passage from ancient and modern Stoic texts, and three core practices: predicting misfortune, examining judgements, daily review. Each presents a new text, and participants complete the practices in the form of a structure daily journal.

OR 


Active Control - Participants will be presented with a passage of text selected from classic and modern fiction. Participants will be instructed to summarise the plot and key points of the passages each day.
table.measured_variables:
-	Stoic ideation: Stoic attitudes and Beliefs Scale (SABS)
-	Subjective units of distress (SUDS scale).
-	Self-reported anxiety: Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item (GAD-7), State Trait Anxiety Inventory-State (STAI-S).
-	General self-efficacy scale (GSE).
-	Brief Resilience scale (BRS).
-      MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status (MacArthur SSS Scale)
-	Connon-Davidson Resilience Scale 10-item (CDRISC-10)
-	Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS-12)
-       Fear of Negative Evaluation (BFNE) scale
-       Ruminative Response Scale-10 (RRS-10)
-       Perceived Stress Scale (PSS)
-       Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ)
-       Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale-16 (DERS-16)
-	Physiological measures of arousal: heart rate, heart rate variability, skin conductance response, and blood pressure with the Biopac MP36. Physiological arousal will be collected prior, during, and after the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST, Kirschbaum, Pirke, & Helhammer, 1993).
table.statistical_tests:
Apart from two exceptions, we will investigate all hypotheses with simple linear regression analyses. Score at post-training will be set as the DV, with baseline score and group entered as predictors. For physiological data (heart rate, heart rate variability, and skin conductance) our outcome will be set as measurement taken during the TSST, with baseline recording and intervention group as the predictor variables.

For blood pressure and SUDS outcomes however, we will conduct one-tailed independent samples t-tests on the difference scores between baseline and post-TSST measures.
table.inference_criteria: Significance will be accepted at the p < .05 level, though we will also include confidence intervals and effect sizes when making inferences about weight of evidence for an effect.
table.missing_data_handling: Missing data will be assessed for randomness with Little’s Test (Little, 1989). Should missing data be related to baseline variables, we will conduct sensitivity analyses adjusting for these variables and reporting the differences. Secondly, we will impute the missing data using multiple imputation by chained equations and re-run the analyses, reporting differences.
table.exploratory_analyses: Whilst we do not specify hypotheses, for transparency we state our intention to explore the effect of STAR on anxiety, rumination, stress, intolerance of uncertainty and emotion regulation.
table.sample_size: We will aim to recruit as many participants as possible through May 12, 2026. Our minimum sample size is 80 participants, but we will aim to maximize sample size.
table.stopping_rule: We will terminate data collection on May 12 2026.

stat_check.summary_text: 1 possible error in t-tests or F-tests

table.text: In support of preregistered Hypothesis 1a, Stoic training was associated with lower posttraining fear of negative evaluation after adjustment for pretraining BFNE scores, b = -2.77, SE = 1.13, t(95) = -2.45, p = .016, 95% CI [-5.01, -0.53], adjusted d = -0.50.

After adjustment for baseline SUDS, participants assigned to Stoic training reported numerically higher SUDS during the TSST, but the condition effect was not statistically significant, b = 3.77, SE = 3.56, t(76) = 1.06, p = .293, 95% CI [-3.33, 10.87], adjusted d = 0.24.

Although the mean increase in STAI-S scores from before to after the TSST was smaller in the Stoic training condition (2.65 points) than in the control condition (5.41 points), the preregistered onetailed Welch's t test did not indicate a significant between-condition difference, t(63.92) = 1.24, p = .109, adjusted d = -.29.

Contrary to preregistered Hypothesis 1c, Stoic training was associated with higher rather than lower heart rate during the TSST after adjustment for baseline heart rate, b = 4.13, SE = 1.95, t(63) = 2.12, p = .038, 95% CI [0.24, 8.02], adjusted d = 0.53.

After adjustment for baseline HRV, Stoic training was associated with lower HRV during the TSST, although the effect narrowly missed the preregistered threshold for statistical significance, b = -0.17, SE = 0.08, t(63) = -1.97, p = .053, 95% CI [-0.335, 0.002], adjusted d = -0.49.
Stoic training was associated with higher posttraining SABS scores after adjustment for pretraining SABS scores, b = 6.06, SE = 2.88, t(95) = 2.11, p = .038, 95% CI [0.35, 11.78], adjusted d = 0.43.
Significant Condition × Phase interactions emerged for both heart rate, F(5, 328.02) = 2.83, p = .016, and HRV, F(5, 328.10) = 2.81, p = .017.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p < .1", "ps > .130", "p < .05", "p < .05", "p < .05", "p < .05", "ps ≥ .360"), Text = c("In cases of significant differences or meeting our prespecified p < .1 sensitivity analysis criterion, we conducted sensitivity analyses with those variables included as covariates.", "The Stoic training and control conditions did not differ significantly on any pretraining self-report measure, all ps > .130.", "CD-RISC scores also increased within the control condition at the p < .05 significance threshold, but this change did not survive correction.", "Stoic Mindfulness also increased at the p < .05 significance threshold but did not survive correction.", "Within the control condition, Beliefs About Happiness decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold but did not remain significant after correction.", "Follow-up contrast suggested that Stoic training participants exhibited a larger increase from pre-baseline to post-TSST when evaluating significance at the p < .05 level, b = 7.40, SE = 3.62, t = 2.04, raw p = .042, but this effect did not remain significant after Hommel correction, adjusted p = .175.", "Adjustment for the interval between training completion and the laboratory visit also did not meaningfully alter the TSST findings: the HR effect remained significant, p = .045, the HRV effect remained similar in magnitude but nonsignificant, p = .062, and the interval itself was unrelated to the laboratory outcomes, all ps ≥ .360." )), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .053", "p = .061", "p = .072", "p < .1 ", "ps > .130", "p = stat_effect_size.summary_text: We found 3 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

table.text: In support of preregistered Hypothesis 1a, Stoic training was associated with lower posttraining fear of negative evaluation after adjustment for pretraining BFNE scores, b = -2.77, SE = 1.13, t(95) = -2.45, p = .016, 95% CI [-5.01, -0.53], adjusted d = -0.50.
table.d_coherence_note: Match under independent-samples equal-n assumption (n1 = n2 = 48.5, N = 97).

table.text: After adjustment for baseline SUDS, participants assigned to Stoic training reported numerically higher SUDS during the TSST, but the condition effect was not statistically significant, b = 3.77, SE = 3.56, t(76) = 1.06, p = .293, 95% CI [-3.33, 10.87], adjusted d = 0.24.
table.d_coherence_note: Match under independent-samples equal-n assumption (n1 = n2 = 39, N = 78).

table.text: Although the mean increase in STAI-S scores from before to after the TSST was smaller in the Stoic training condition (2.65 points) than in the control condition (5.41 points), the preregistered onetailed Welch's t test did not indicate a significant between-condition difference, t(63.92) = 1.24, p = .109, adjusted d = -.29.
table.d_coherence_note: Non-integer df indicates Welch's t-test (unequal variances); sample sizes cannot be determined.

table.text: Contrary to preregistered Hypothesis 1c, Stoic training was associated with higher rather than lower heart rate during the TSST after adjustment for baseline heart rate, b = 4.13, SE = 1.95, t(63) = 2.12, p = .038, 95% CI [0.24, 8.02], adjusted d = 0.53.
table.d_coherence_note: Match under independent-samples equal-n assumption (n1 = n2 = 32.5, N = 65).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 586 columns across 6 data files.
#### Issues Identified

10 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("?view_only=d2442d6e43fb432bb00e817823a14e72: Study Data/Lab_SelfReport_deidentified.csv", "?view_only=d2442d6e43fb432bb00e817823a14e72: Study Data/Lab_SelfReport_deidentified.csv", "?view_only=d2442d6e43fb432bb00e817823a14e72: Study Data/Lab_SelfReport_deidentified.csv", "?view_only=d2442d6e43fb432bb00e817823a14e72: Study Data/Lab_SelfReport_deidentified.csv", "?view_only=d2442d6e43fb432bb00e817823a14e72: Study Data/Lab_SelfReport_deidentified.csv", "d3ex4: Study Data/Lab_SelfReport_deidentified.csv", "d3ex4: Study Data/Lab_SelfReport_deidentified.csv", "d3ex4: Study Data/Lab_SelfReport_deidentified.csv", "d3ex4: Study Data/Lab_SelfReport_deidentified.csv", "d3ex4: Study Data/Lab_SelfReport_deidentified.csv"), Column = c("LVF5_transcribed", "Other_explain", "RA2_encourages_explain", "RA3_encourages_explain", "TSST_RAs_rate_transcribed", "LVF5_transcribed", "Other_explain", "RA2_encourages_explain", "RA3_encourages_explain", "TSST_RAs_rate_transcribed" ), Issues = c("#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 96% numeric but 3 values cannot be parsed: \"7-8 ish\", \"8-...", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 104 characters, 91% distinct) may contain ...
↔️ Whitespace — 5 values with leading/trailing whitespace: \"The participant keeps m...", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 96% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"noded twice\"", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 96% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"nodded\"", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 83% numeric but 11 values cannot be parsed: \"RA2/RA3: 3\",...", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 96% numeric but 3 values cannot be parsed: \"7-8 ish\", \"8-...", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 104 characters, 91% distinct) may contain ...
↔️ Whitespace — 5 values with leading/trailing whitespace: \"The participant keeps m...", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 96% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"noded twice\"", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 96% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"nodded\"", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 83% numeric but 11 values cannot be parsed: \"RA2/RA3: 3\",..." )), row.names = c(NA, -10L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No respondent was flagged for straightlining in the 2 files that could be screened.

**What this does not cover.** Only 2 of 6 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Undergraduate students (M age = 19.16 years, SD = 1.05; 81% women) were randomized to eight days of online Stoic training or an active control involving literary-fiction readings.
Ninety-eight participants completed pretraining and posttraining self-report assessments (Stoic training, n = 46; control, n = 52).
Participants were 98 undergraduate students recruited via the Hamilton College online recruitment system.
As compensation, participants were offered extra credit in their eligible psychology and neuroscience courses.

Participants were selected based on their scores on the Brief Resilience Scale (BRS; Smith et al. 2008), with applicants scoring greater than 4.3 out of 5 being excluded in order to decrease the likelihood of a ceiling effect.
Participants were randomly allocated to either Stoic Training (pre-training n = 61, post-training n = 46) or Active Control (pre-training n = 60, post-training n = 52).
Participants were not informed that the study involved multiple experimental conditions or that they were receiving an intervention.
After completing the training period, participants completed the same self-report questionnaires administered at baseline.
Participants were then invited to schedule a laboratory visit and were encouraged to attend within four calendar days of completing their assigned training or control activities.
Prior to the lab visit, participants were asked to refrain from caffeine for 6 hours, alcohol for 12 hours, and food and vigorous exercise for 3 hours.
During the lab visit, participants completed brief pre-task questionnaires to measure adherence to protocol and baseline state anxiety.
After completing self-report forms, participants were connected to physiological recording equipment, completed a modified TSST, and self-reported post-TSST state anxiety.
Participants were instructed to complete the eight sessions within 12 days, although additional time was permitted when necessary.

Participants completed the Stoic Attitudes and Behaviours Scale to measure Stoicism as a life philosophy (SABS; LeBon et al., 2026), Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation Scale to measure fear of negative evaluation (BFNE; Leary 1983), the Ruminative Response Scale-10 to measure rumination (RRS-10; Treynor et al., 2003), the General Self-Efficacy Scale to measure selfefficacy (GSE; Schwarzer & Jerusalem 1995), the Brief Resilience Scale to measure resilience as the ability to bounce back from stress (BRS; Smith et al. 2008), and the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale-10 to measure resilience as perceived ability to cope with and adapt to adversity (CD-RISC-10; Campbell-Sills and Stein 2007).
Participants completed a modified version of the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST; Kirschbaum et al., 1993), a standardized laboratory stressor designed to elicit social-evaluative threat.

During this phase, participants assigned to Stoic training were instructed to apply the practice of Negative Visualization to the upcoming social stress task during a 5-minute period, whereas participants assigned to the control condition were instructed to wait quietly for 5 minutes.
For the speech task, participants were instructed to give a speech about why they were qualified for their dream job in front of two evaluative panelists.
For the mental arithmetic task, participants were instructed to serially subtract 13 from 1,022 as quickly and accurately as possible and to start over if they made an error.

However, for GSR, frequent electrode detachment resulted in unreliable signal quality, and no standardized procedure was available to determine consistently which participants had provided usable recordings.

Participants were encouraged to attend the laboratory visit within four calendar days of completing their assigned training or control activities, although later visits were permitted when scheduling within this window was not feasible.

After adjustment for baseline SUDS, participants assigned to Stoic training reported numerically higher SUDS during the TSST, but the condition effect was not statistically significant, b = 3.77, SE = 3.56, t(76) = 1.06, p = .293, 95% CI [-3.33, 10.87], adjusted d = 0.24.

Contrary to prediction, participants assigned to Stoic training exhibited higher baseline-adjusted HR during the TSST and lower baseline-adjusted HRV, although the preregistered HRV effect narrowly missed the conventional significance threshold.

Participants in the Stoic condition had completed eight sessions of internet-delivered Stoic training and then engaged in five minutes of Negative Visualization immediately before receiving the speech instructions, whereas control participants completed eight sessions of the active control and spent the corresponding five-minute period waiting quietly.
All participants had complete item-level data for the measures shown.
All participants had complete item-level data for the subscales shown.

#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 8 scripts: 0 ran without error, 8 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

text.text: Purpose Stoic philosophy has influenced cognitive and behavioral therapies, but Stoic training has received limited empirical evaluation.

This preregistered randomized controlled trial examined whether Stoic training reduced fear of negative evaluation (FNE), improved broader psychological outcomes, increased Stoic attitudes and behaviors, and altered subjective and cardiac responses to acute social-evaluative stress.
Undergraduate students (M age = 19.16 years, SD = 1.05; 81% women) were randomized to eight days of online Stoic training or an active control involving literary-fiction readings.
Ninety-eight participants completed pretraining and posttraining self-report assessments (Stoic training, n = 46; control, n = 52).
Seventy-eight subsequently completed a modified Trier Social Stress Test (TSST), of whom 66 provided usable electrocardiography data for the preregistered cardiac analyses.
Before speech preparation, participants in the Stoic condition completed a five-minute Negative Visualization exercise, whereas control participants waited quietly.

Relative to the active control, Stoic training was associated with lower posttraining FNE when controlling for pretraining scores, b = -2.77, p = .016, adjusted d = -0.50, and higher posttraining Stoic Attitudes and Behaviours Scale scores, b = 6.06, p = .038, adjusted d = 0.43.
Exploratory subscale analyses suggested possible effects on Beliefs About Control and Beliefs About Happiness, although neither remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons.
Between-condition effects on resilience, self-efficacy, and rumination were not significant.

During the TSST, cardiac effects were contrary to prediction: Stoic training was associated with higher heart rate, b = 4.13, p = .038, adjusted d = 0.53, and lower heart rate variability, although the latter effect narrowly missed statistical significance, b = -0.17, p = .053, adjusted d = -0.49.
Subjective distress and state-anxiety responses to the TSST did not differ significantly by condition.

Conclusions Stoic training led to significantly greater reductions in FNE and increases in Stoic attitudes than an active control, whereas broader psychological outcomes did not differ significantly between conditions.

These findings provide initial evidence that brief Stoic training may modify a cognitive vulnerability relevant to social evaluation while engaging the attitudes and behaviors it is intended to cultivate.

The unexpected cardiac effects may reflect the broader training, the acute Negative Visualization exercise administered before the stressor, or their combination, highlighting the need to disentangle the cumulative and acute effects of Stoic practice and determine how the timing and context of Negative Visualization influence responses to social-evaluative stress.
Anxiety and other mental health problems have increased substantially among U.S. college students over the past two decades (Duffy et al., 2019; Nails et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Anxiety and other mental health problems have increased substantially among U.S. college students over the past two decades <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Duffy et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Nails et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These difficulties can interfere with academic performance, interpersonal relationships, and quality of life, yet many students experiencing psychological distress do not receive formal treatment (Eisenberg et al., 2011; Lipson et al., 2022).
text.formatted: These difficulties can interfere with academic performance, interpersonal relationships, and quality of life, yet many students experiencing psychological distress do not receive formal treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Eisenberg et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Lipson et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, there is a need for brief and scalable interventions that can be administered before psychological difficulties become severe.
Fear of negative evaluation (FNE), defined as apprehension about and concern over others' negative judgments, may be a particularly important target for early intervention in college populations.
Cognitive and neurobiological research identifies FNE as a core feature of social anxiety disorder (Birk et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Cognitive and neurobiological research identifies FNE as a core feature of social anxiety disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Birk et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Gao et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Social-evaluative fears may be especially consequential during college, where academic participation, relationship formation, and entry into new social networks frequently involve interpersonal evaluation; elevated social anxiety symptoms have accordingly been associated with functional impairment and poorer academic achievement among university students (Brook & Willoughby, 2015; Dell'Osso et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Social-evaluative fears may be especially consequential during college, where academic participation, relationship formation, and entry into new social networks frequently involve interpersonal evaluation; elevated social anxiety symptoms have accordingly been associated with functional impairment and poorer academic achievement among university students <ref type="bibr">(Brook & Willoughby, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Dell'Osso et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, social-evaluative fears vary dimensionally and can interfere with functioning across a broad range of symptom severity, suggesting that the consequences of FNE and related concerns extend below the diagnostic threshold (Busch et al., 2023; Dell'Osso et al., 2014; Ruscio et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Importantly, social-evaluative fears vary dimensionally and can interfere with functioning across a broad range of symptom severity, suggesting that the consequences of FNE and related concerns extend below the diagnostic threshold <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Busch et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Dell'Osso et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Ruscio et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, FNE represents both a central feature of social anxiety disorder and a dimensional cognitive vulnerability relevant to student mental health and well-being.
Cognitive models propose that social-evaluative fears are maintained partly by maladaptive interpretations of social situations.

Individuals with elevated social anxiety may overestimate the likelihood or consequences of negative social outcomes, assume that visible anxiety or imperfect performance will lead to rejection, and evaluate themselves according to excessively demanding standards (e.g., Clark & Wells, 1995; Rapee & Heimberg, 1997).
text.formatted: Individuals with elevated social anxiety may overestimate the likelihood or consequences of negative social outcomes, assume that visible anxiety or imperfect performance will lead to rejection, and evaluate themselves according to excessively demanding standards (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Clark & Wells, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rapee & Heimberg, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Particularly relevant to the present study, they may treat unfavorable evaluation as highly consequential or intolerable and devote substantial effort to controlling how they are perceived (Clark & Wells, 1995; Hofmann, 2007; Rapee & Heimberg, 1997).
text.formatted: Particularly relevant to the present study, they may treat unfavorable evaluation as highly consequential or intolerable and devote substantial effort to controlling how they are perceived <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clark & Wells, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Hofmann, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rapee & Heimberg, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: These appraisals can promote maladaptive threat-focused anticipatory processing, post-event rumination, self-focused attention, and avoidance (Clark & Wells, 1995; Mellings & Alden, 2000; Rapee & Heimberg, 1997).
text.formatted: These appraisals can promote maladaptive threat-focused anticipatory processing, post-event rumination, self-focused attention, and avoidance <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clark & Wells, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Mellings & Alden, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rapee & Heimberg, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Daily-process research illustrates how these mechanisms operate among college students: on days characterized by greater FNE, students also report greater maladaptive anticipatory processing, post-event rumination, and social withdrawal (Campbell et al., 2016), which in turn may form a self-reinforcing pattern.
text.formatted: Daily-process research illustrates how these mechanisms operate among college students: on days characterized by greater FNE, students also report greater maladaptive anticipatory processing, post-event rumination, and social withdrawal <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Campbell et al., 2016)</ref>, which in turn may form a self-reinforcing pattern.

text.text: Maladaptive anticipatory processing can heighten anxiety before and during a social encounter when it involves repetitive predictions of embarrassment or rejection, negative self-imagery, and doubts about one's ability to manage an unfavorable outcome, with little corresponding focus on constructive ways of responding to possible difficulties (Clark & Wells, 1995; Hinrichsen & Clark, 2003).
text.formatted: Maladaptive anticipatory processing can heighten anxiety before and during a social encounter when it involves repetitive predictions of embarrassment or rejection, negative self-imagery, and doubts about one's ability to manage an unfavorable outcome, with little corresponding focus on constructive ways of responding to possible difficulties <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clark & Wells, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Hinrichsen & Clark, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Meanwhile, post-event rumination can sustain distress, exacerbate social anxiety symptoms, and strengthen negative expectations (Clark & Wells, 1995; Edgar et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Meanwhile, post-event rumination can sustain distress, exacerbate social anxiety symptoms, and strengthen negative expectations <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clark & Wells, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Edgar et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, although withdrawal can provide shortterm relief, it ultimately limits opportunities to learn that unfavorable outcomes may be manageable and that effective action remains possible despite uncertainty (Hofmann, 2007).
text.formatted: Moreover, although withdrawal can provide shortterm relief, it ultimately limits opportunities to learn that unfavorable outcomes may be manageable and that effective action remains possible despite uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Hofmann, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Because FNE is linked to these proximal cognitive and behavioral processes, it is a promising target for preventive intervention.

A growing literature has evaluated brief and scalable cognitive-behavioral approaches to social anxiety and FNE among college students, although evidence for reductions in broad FNE and generalization to acute social-evaluative responding remains mixed.

Established cognitivebehavioral interventions address social anxiety by helping individuals examine catastrophic predictions, reduce attempts to control how they are perceived, redirect attention away from internal threat monitoring, and engage with feared situations despite uncertainty (Clark & Wells, 1995; Hofmann, 2007).
text.formatted: Established cognitivebehavioral interventions address social anxiety by helping individuals examine catastrophic predictions, reduce attempts to control how they are perceived, redirect attention away from internal threat monitoring, and engage with feared situations despite uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clark & Wells, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Hofmann, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Digitally delivered approaches provide a potentially scalable means of making these strategies available to college students (Harrer et al., 2019; Oliveira et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Digitally delivered approaches provide a potentially scalable means of making these strategies available to college students <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Harrer et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Oliveira et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Internet-based CBT has been found to reduce social anxiety symptoms among university students relative to a waitlist control (McCall et al., 2018; Kählke et al., 2019), with one such study also reporting a significant between-group reduction in broad FNE (McCall et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Internet-based CBT has been found to reduce social anxiety symptoms among university students relative to a waitlist control <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(McCall et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Kählke et al., 2019)</ref>, with one such study also reporting a significant between-group reduction in broad FNE <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(McCall et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, a six-session smartphone-based hypnosis intervention produced a significantly greater reduction in broad FNE among undergraduates with elevated shyness than a no-treatment control (Ma et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Similarly, a six-session smartphone-based hypnosis intervention produced a significantly greater reduction in broad FNE among undergraduates with elevated shyness than a no-treatment control <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Ma et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Brief face-to-face approaches provide additional evidence that FNE may be modifiable over relatively short periods, including a three-day intensive group CBT program that produced reductions in FNE relative to a waitlist control (Cui & Tang, 2026).
text.formatted: Brief face-to-face approaches provide additional evidence that FNE may be modifiable over relatively short periods, including a three-day intensive group CBT program that produced reductions in FNE relative to a waitlist control <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cui & Tang, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These studies help establish brief and digital interventions for FNE as promising in college students, but one important limitation of the above-mentioned digital intervention studies is the use of a waitlist or no-treatment control.

Brief intervention and digital intervention studies that have used an active (rather than waitlist or no treatment) control have found inconsistent effects on FNE, and evidence for reductions in broad FNE among college students remains especially limited.

In an RCT of a brief in-person intervention comparing six-session group exposure and response prevention with an educational-support active control among college students, FNE changes did not differ significantly between conditions, despite a significant intervention effect on social anxiety (Zaboski et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In an RCT of a brief in-person intervention comparing six-session group exposure and response prevention with an educational-support active control among college students, FNE changes did not differ significantly between conditions, despite a significant intervention effect on social anxiety <ref type="bibr">(Zaboski et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Project Engage, a self-guided digital single-session intervention designed to help college students cope with FNE in active-learning science courses, increased immediate confidence in small-group and whole-class participation; however, broad FNE was assessed only at baseline, and outcomes were classroom-specific (Ghosh et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Project Engage, a self-guided digital single-session intervention designed to help college students cope with FNE in active-learning science courses, increased immediate confidence in small-group and whole-class participation; however, broad FNE was assessed only at baseline, and outcomes were classroom-specific <ref type="bibr">(Ghosh et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Online Cognitive Bias Modification for Interpretation (CBM-I) has also been examined as a preventive intervention during the transition to college.

Among students anxious about beginning university, five online CBM-I sessions produced a significantly greater reduction in broad FNE from baseline to the first day of university than an expectancy-matched active control involving neutral visuospatial brain-training tasks (Hoppitt et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Among students anxious about beginning university, five online CBM-I sessions produced a significantly greater reduction in broad FNE from baseline to the first day of university than an expectancy-matched active control involving neutral visuospatial brain-training tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Hoppitt et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: This finding demonstrates that a brief online intervention can reduce FNE in anticipation of the transition to university; however, because training occurred before the semester and the between-condition difference was not significant four weeks later, it remains unclear whether comparable effects would emerge or remain evident when an intervention is delivered amid ongoing academic and social-evaluative demands (Hoppitt et al., 2014).
text.formatted: This finding demonstrates that a brief online intervention can reduce FNE in anticipation of the transition to university; however, because training occurred before the semester and the between-condition difference was not significant four weeks later, it remains unclear whether comparable effects would emerge or remain evident when an intervention is delivered amid ongoing academic and social-evaluative demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Hoppitt et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: More recently, in a community sample of adults with elevated social anxiety that was not specific to college students, a six-session online CBM-I led to a significantly greater decrease in FNE relative to an active control when measured one week after the end of the intervention period (although the between-group effect immediately after training narrowly missed significance) (Abado et al., 2026).
text.formatted: More recently, in a community sample of adults with elevated social anxiety that was not specific to college students, a six-session online CBM-I led to a significantly greater decrease in FNE relative to an active control when measured one week after the end of the intervention period (although the between-group effect immediately after training narrowly missed significance) <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abado et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, brief and scalable interventions have shown promise, but evidence remains limited regarding whether a scalable digital intervention with broader cognitive targets can produce between-group reductions in broad FNE in college students, particularly when comparing to an active control and when delivered amid ongoing academic and social-evaluative demands.
Stoic training may provide a promising broad cognitive approach to decrease FNE in college students, but to our knowledge the effects of Stoic training on FNE have yet to be evaluated.

Although the word "stoic" is colloquially used to refer to suppression of emotional expression and has historically been used similarly in portions of the psychological literature, philosophical Stoicism encourages awareness of emotional reactions and deliberate examination of the judgments that shape them (Karl et al., 2022; LeBon et al., 2026; Murray et al., 2008; Pathak et al., 2017; MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021).
text.formatted: Although the word "stoic" is colloquially used to refer to suppression of emotional expression and has historically been used similarly in portions of the psychological literature, philosophical Stoicism encourages awareness of emotional reactions and deliberate examination of the judgments that shape them <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Karl et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">LeBon et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Murray et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Pathak et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, philosophical Stoicism emphasizes understanding and regulating emotion rather than denial or suppression (Karl et al., 2022; MacLellan & Lewis, 2026).
text.formatted: Thus, philosophical Stoicism emphasizes understanding and regulating emotion rather than denial or suppression <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Karl et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">MacLellan & Lewis, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Preliminary evaluations conducted by the Modern Stoicism organization have reported within-group pre-to-post-intervention improvements in well-being, resilience, and Stoic attitudes following large-scale online programs such as Stoic Week and Stoic Mindfulness and Resilience Training, although these findings are limited by self-selection, attrition, the absence of control conditions, and publication outside the peer-reviewed literature (LeBon, 2018 (LeBon, , 2020)).
text.formatted: Preliminary evaluations conducted by the Modern Stoicism organization have reported within-group pre-to-post-intervention improvements in well-being, resilience, and Stoic attitudes following large-scale online programs such as Stoic Week and Stoic Mindfulness and Resilience Training, although these findings are limited by self-selection, attrition, the absence of control conditions, and publication outside the peer-reviewed literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(LeBon, 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(LeBon, , 2020))</ref>.

text.text: In the first peer-reviewed RCT of Stoic training, MacLellan and Derakshan (2021) assigned 45 high worriers from a university and the surrounding community to Stoic training, combined Stoic and adaptive working-memory training, or an active working-memory control condition.

Both conditions containing Stoic training produced greater reductions in rumination than the active control, and Stoic training alone produced greater improvements in self-efficacy than the active control.
Text analyses also indicated reductions in anxious and negatively valanced language during training, suggesting changes in cognitive-emotional processing beyond questionnaire outcomes.

In a subsequent study of 24 medical students, Brown et al. (2022) observed within-group increases in Stoic attitudes and behaviors, resilience, and empathy; however, they did not employ a control group.
text.formatted: In a subsequent study of 24 medical students, <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Brown et al. (2022)</ref> observed within-group increases in Stoic attitudes and behaviors, resilience, and empathy; however, they did not employ a control group.

text.text: These findings provide preliminary support for Stoic training, but larger RCTs are needed, particularly for outcomes closely tied to cognitive models of social anxiety in college students such as FNE.
Stoicism contains principles and practices that may be especially relevant to the cognitive processes maintaining FNE.

Broadly, Stoic philosophy emphasizes intentional action, attention to what is under personal control, acceptance of what is outside personal control, and examination of the judgments that contribute to emotional distress.

Two central Stoic principles, the distinction between controllable and uncontrollable events and the proposition that emotional responses are shaped by judgments, have substantial conceptual overlap with the cognitive model underlying cognitive and behavioral therapies (CBT) (Beck, 1976; Ellis, 1962 Ellis, , 2010;; LeBon et al., 2026; Robertson & Codd, 2019).
text.formatted: Two central Stoic principles, the distinction between controllable and uncontrollable events and the proposition that emotional responses are shaped by judgments, have substantial conceptual overlap with the cognitive model underlying cognitive and behavioral therapies (CBT) <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Beck, 1976;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Ellis, 1962</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Ellis, , 2010;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">LeBon et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Robertson & Codd, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In fact, both Ellis and Beck explicitly identified Stoic philosophy as an important precursor to rational-emotive behavior therapy and cognitive therapy, respectively, two foundational traditions within modern CBT, although these approaches subsequently developed as distinct therapeutic systems (Beck et al., 1979; Ellis, 1962 Ellis, , 2010;; Robertson, 2016).
text.formatted: In fact, both Ellis and Beck explicitly identified Stoic philosophy as an important precursor to rational-emotive behavior therapy and cognitive therapy, respectively, two foundational traditions within modern CBT, although these approaches subsequently developed as distinct therapeutic systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Beck et al., 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Ellis, 1962</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Ellis, , 2010;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Robertson, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Applied to social evaluation, Stoic beliefs about control may shift attention away from attempts to manage other people's judgments and toward one's own choices and behavior (LeBon et al., 2026; Robertson & Codd, 2019).
text.formatted: Applied to social evaluation, Stoic beliefs about control may shift attention away from attempts to manage other people's judgments and toward one's own choices and behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(LeBon et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Robertson & Codd, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Relatedly, Stoic beliefs about happiness may weaken the assumption that favorable evaluation is necessary for well-being by treating reputation and social approval as external outcomes that are not essential to flourishing (LeBon et al., 2026; Sellars, 2006).
text.formatted: Relatedly, Stoic beliefs about happiness may weaken the assumption that favorable evaluation is necessary for well-being by treating reputation and social approval as external outcomes that are not essential to flourishing <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(LeBon et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Sellars, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, Stoic practices that emphasize monitoring one's judgments and evaluating oneself according to one's conduct rather than external approval may help individuals identify and reconsider catastrophic assumptions about embarrassment, rejection, or visible anxiety (Clark & Wells, 1995; Hofmann, 2007; Karl, Fischer, & LeBon, 2026; LeBon et al., 2026; Sellars, 2006).
text.formatted: More broadly, Stoic practices that emphasize monitoring one's judgments and evaluating oneself according to one's conduct rather than external approval may help individuals identify and reconsider catastrophic assumptions about embarrassment, rejection, or visible anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clark & Wells, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Hofmann, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Karl, Fischer, & LeBon, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">LeBon et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Sellars, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, Stoic training draws on a philosophical tradition that helped shape foundational cognitive approaches within CBT while presenting these principles within a distinct and broader philosophical and ethical framework.
Previously studied Stoic interventions have combined recurring practices and readings designed to shape how individuals anticipate, interpret, and reflect on challenging experiences.
The two published peer-reviewed Stoic interventions incorporated much of the same core content, with Brown et al. (2022) additionally including an empathy module.
text.formatted: The two published peer-reviewed Stoic interventions incorporated much of the same core content, with <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Brown et al. (2022)</ref> additionally including an empathy module.

text.text: Both interventions used three recurring daily practices: Negative Visualization, Stoic Mindfulness, and Stoic Reflectionfoot_0 .
text.formatted: Both interventions used three recurring daily practices: Negative Visualization, Stoic Mindfulness, and Stoic Reflection<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> .

text.text: Another shared element was daily readings that introduced Stoic concepts and prompted participants to summarize, reflect on, and apply the material (Brown et al., 2022; MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021).
text.formatted: Another shared element was daily readings that introduced Stoic concepts and prompted participants to summarize, reflect on, and apply the material <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brown et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Collectively, these components repeatedly target how individuals anticipate, interpret, and reflect on challenging experiences.

Negative Visualization involves intentionally considering the possibility that an unwanted outcome could occur and preparing to cope with or respond constructively to it, rather than relying on reassurance that it will not happen (Brown et al., 2022; MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021).
text.formatted: Negative Visualization involves intentionally considering the possibility that an unwanted outcome could occur and preparing to cope with or respond constructively to it, rather than relying on reassurance that it will not happen <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brown et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: It therefore differs conceptually from the maladaptive anticipatory processing implicated in social anxiety, which often centers on threat, catastrophic predictions, and perceived inability to cope (Clark & Wells, 1995; Hofmann, 2007), by pairing consideration of possible adverse outcomes with deliberate preparation for practical action and emotional coping.
text.formatted: It therefore differs conceptually from the maladaptive anticipatory processing implicated in social anxiety, which often centers on threat, catastrophic predictions, and perceived inability to cope <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clark & Wells, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Hofmann, 2007)</ref>, by pairing consideration of possible adverse outcomes with deliberate preparation for practical action and emotional coping.

text.text: Stoic Mindfulness involves identifying one's judgments, distinguishing them from the events or initial impressions on which they are based, and examining the sequence of experiences and interpretations that gave rise to them.

Stoic Reflection involves reviewing one's thoughts and actions from the day, identifying behaviors or responses that were unhelpful, considering opportunities or duties that were left unaddressed, recognizing what was done well, and reflecting on how one might respond more intentionally in the future.

The rotating readings broaden these practices and situate them within a coherent Stoic philosophical framework by introducing additional Stoic principles and asking participants to apply them to their own experiences (Brown et al., 2022; MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021).
text.formatted: The rotating readings broaden these practices and situate them within a coherent Stoic philosophical framework by introducing additional Stoic principles and asking participants to apply them to their own experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brown et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Although these practices are designed to address stressful experiences broadly, they may be especially well suited to reducing FNE among college students, who routinely encounter situations involving social scrutiny and the possibility of unfavorable judgment.

In socially evaluative contexts, these practices may weaken assumptions that embarrassment, criticism, or unfavorable judgments would be intolerable, reduce efforts to control others' impressions, and strengthen perceived capacity to respond effectively when unfavorable evaluation cannot be prevented.
Across repeated practice, Stoic training may therefore reduce FNE by fostering more adaptive ways of anticipating, interpreting, and reflecting on socially evaluative experiences.

Classical Stoic texts and recent psychological evidence suggest that Negative Visualization may be particularly relevant to FNE, but the specific time course and effects on broad FNE versus acute social-evaluative stress are not clear.
Negative Visualization can be applied prospectively before the precise form of an anticipated social challenge is known.

In Meditations, Marcus Aurelius prepares himself to encounter difficult interpersonal behavior without knowing precisely when or how it will occur and rehearses his intended response (Meditations, 2.1).

Epictetus similarly advises practitioners to consider the difficulties commonly associated with an activity before undertaking it and to prepare their response (Enchiridion, 4), while Seneca argues that adversity has a gentler impact when considered beforehand because part of its disruptive force derives from novelty (Moral Letters, 76.33-34).

Consistent with this rationale, participants in a prior Stoic training intervention qualitatively described Negative Visualization as helping them anticipate difficulties, develop contingency plans, reduce uncertainty, and avoid catastrophizing when events did not proceed as expected (Brown et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Consistent with this rationale, participants in a prior Stoic training intervention qualitatively described Negative Visualization as helping them anticipate difficulties, develop contingency plans, reduce uncertainty, and avoid catastrophizing when events did not proceed as expected <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brown et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, the effects of Negative Visualization may nevertheless differ between broad FNE and immediate acute responses to social evaluation.

Across the intervention period, repeated Stoic practice may weaken relatively enduring beliefs that unfavorable evaluation would be intolerable and increase confidence in coping with negative social outcomes, consistent with preliminary evidence that Stoic training may promote preparedness and self-efficacy more broadly (Brown et al., 2022; MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021).
text.formatted: Across the intervention period, repeated Stoic practice may weaken relatively enduring beliefs that unfavorable evaluation would be intolerable and increase confidence in coping with negative social outcomes, consistent with preliminary evidence that Stoic training may promote preparedness and self-efficacy more broadly <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brown et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: When practiced immediately before a social stressor, Negative Visualization could similarly reduce surprise and uncertainty, increase preparedness, and thereby lessen acute emotional reactivity (Brown et al., 2022).
text.formatted: When practiced immediately before a social stressor, Negative Visualization could similarly reduce surprise and uncertainty, increase preparedness, and thereby lessen acute emotional reactivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brown et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, contemplating possible failure could also temporarily increase threat salience and anticipatory arousal (Makkar & Grisham, 2011; Schulz et al., 2008), particularly among individuals who have had limited time to consolidate the broader Stoic framework.
text.formatted: However, contemplating possible failure could also temporarily increase threat salience and anticipatory arousal <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Makkar & Grisham, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Schulz et al., 2008)</ref>, particularly among individuals who have had limited time to consolidate the broader Stoic framework.

text.text: To our knowledge, no prior study has examined the physiological effects of a Stoic intervention.
Of note, evidence that intervention-related improvements in broad FNE extend to acute reactivity during social evaluation also remains limited.

For example, although online CBM-I produced a significantly greater reduction in broad FNE in adults than an active control at follow-up, it did not alter HR or HRV responses to a social-evaluative performance task administered after training (Abado et al., 2026).
text.formatted: For example, although online CBM-I produced a significantly greater reduction in broad FNE in adults than an active control at follow-up, it did not alter HR or HRV responses to a social-evaluative performance task administered after training <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abado et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, is important to determine whether Stoic training alters broad FNE, immediate subjective distress, and cardiac responses during acute social evaluation in parallel or produces divergent effects across these outcomes.
The Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) is well suited to examine acute subjective and cardiac responses.

Heart rate (HR) reflects autonomic mobilization during stress, arising from increased sympathetic influence, parasympathetic withdrawal, or both, whereas heart rate variability (HRV), particularly when indexed by the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD), primarily reflects parasympathetic, or vagal, modulation of the heart (Berntson et al., 1997; Laborde et al., 2017; Quigley et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Heart rate (HR) reflects autonomic mobilization during stress, arising from increased sympathetic influence, parasympathetic withdrawal, or both, whereas heart rate variability (HRV), particularly when indexed by the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD), primarily reflects parasympathetic, or vagal, modulation of the heart <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Berntson et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Laborde et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Quigley et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Within the neurovisceral integration framework, greater resting vagally mediated HRV is associated with more flexible top-down regulation of autonomic, cognitive, and emotional responses (Thayer et al., 2009 (Thayer et al., , 2012)).
text.formatted: Within the neurovisceral integration framework, greater resting vagally mediated HRV is associated with more flexible top-down regulation of autonomic, cognitive, and emotional responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Thayer et al., 2009</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Thayer et al., , 2012))</ref>.

text.text: Lower subjective distress accompanied by attenuated HR reactivity and greater HRV would therefore be broadly consistent with reduced stress responding and more flexible autonomic regulation (Laborde et al., 2017; Thayer et al., 2009 Thayer et al., , 2012)).
text.formatted: Lower subjective distress accompanied by attenuated HR reactivity and greater HRV would therefore be broadly consistent with reduced stress responding and more flexible autonomic regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Laborde et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Thayer et al., 2009</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Thayer et al., , 2012))</ref>.

text.text: However, the magnitude and direction of cardiovascular responses during acute stress do not have a one-to-one psychological interpretation.

Greater HR activation during acute stress may accompany heightened threat responding, effort mobilization, or active engagement with a demanding task rather than distress alone (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010; Ginty et al., 2022; Seery, 2011).
text.formatted: Greater HR activation during acute stress may accompany heightened threat responding, effort mobilization, or active engagement with a demanding task rather than distress alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Ginty et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Seery, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Likewise, lower HRV during acute stress may accompany heightened stress or threat reactivity, increased cognitive or regulatory demand, or more effortful responding during the task (Delliaux et al., 2019; Laborde et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Likewise, lower HRV during acute stress may accompany heightened stress or threat reactivity, increased cognitive or regulatory demand, or more effortful responding during the task <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Delliaux et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Laborde et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Comparing subjective distress with the magnitude and timing of HR and HRV responses across the TSST may therefore help distinguish whether Stoic training attenuates social-evaluative stress, alters engagement with the stressor, or produces partially divergent subjective and physiological effects.
In addition to evaluating distal psychological outcomes, it is important to determine whether Stoic training impacts the attitudes and behaviors it is intended to cultivate.

Prior studies have reported within-group increases in Stoic attitudes following training, but the evidence remains limited: Brown et al. (2022) did not include a control group, and MacLellan and Derakshan (2021) did not observe a statistically significant between-group difference.
text.formatted: Prior studies have reported within-group increases in Stoic attitudes following training, but the evidence remains limited: <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Brown et al. (2022)</ref> did not include a control group, and MacLellan and Derakshan (2021) did not observe a statistically significant between-group difference.

text.text: The recently validated Stoic Attitudes and Behaviours Scale (SABS) was developed specifically to assess philosophical Stoicism rather than colloquial 'stoicism' (i.e., emotional suppression).

Validation in more than 8,000 participants supported a 40-item measure comprising seven related dimensions: beliefs about happiness, Stoic mindfulness, virtue, benevolence and compassion, beliefs about control, ethical development, and Stoic worldview (LeBon et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Validation in more than 8,000 participants supported a 40-item measure comprising seven related dimensions: beliefs about happiness, Stoic mindfulness, virtue, benevolence and compassion, beliefs about control, ethical development, and Stoic worldview <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(LeBon et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, change in total SABS scores may provide an index of overall intervention target engagement, while the subscales may clarify whether changes were broadly distributed across SABS or concentrated in particular facets.

Moreover, recent cross-sectional evidence linking higher SABS scores with greater well-being, resilience, self-efficacy, cognitive reappraisal, and character strengths, and with lower worry, dysfunctional attitudes, emotion-regulation difficulties, and dysfunctional anger, suggests that the Stoic attitudes and behaviors assessed by the SABS may represent a psychologically meaningful intervention target with broad relevance to mental health and well-being (Karl & LeBon, 2026; LeBon et al., 2026; MacLellan & Lewis, 2026).

text.text: The present RCT aimed to evaluate the effects of Stoic training on FNE, broader psychological functioning, SABS, and responses to acute social-evaluative stress among college students.
Our primary preregistered research question was as follows: Does Stoic Training bolster resilience to social stress?
Relative to the control condition, we hypothesized that Stoic training would produce lower postintervention FNE when adjusting for preintervention FNE (H1a).
During the TSST, we further hypothesized lower HR (H1b), greater HRV (H1c), and lower subjective distress (H1d) when controlling for their respective baseline levels.
Further, as an additional test of H1d, we also predicted a smaller pre-to post-TSST increase in state anxiety in the Stoic training group.
We also preregistered hypotheses that Stoic training would reduce rumination (H2a) and increase self-efficacy (H2b) and resilience (H2c).

These secondary hypotheses tested whether previously reported benefits of Stoic training for self-efficacy and rumination would replicate in a larger, exclusively undergraduate sample and whether prior within-group evidence for increased resilience would extend to a between-group RCT effect.

Finally, we conducted planned exploratory analyses of the SABS total score and its seven subscales to assess intervention target engagement and identify which Stoic attitudes were most responsive to training.

Overall, the study tested whether a brief, electronically delivered Stoic intervention could influence a theoretically central cognitive vulnerability, its associated acute stress response, broader psychological risk and protective factors, and the Stoic attitudes and behaviors the intervention was designed to cultivate.
