text.text: Participants were 98 undergraduate students recruited via the Hamilton College online recruitment system.
As compensation, participants were offered extra credit in their eligible psychology and neuroscience courses.

Participants were selected based on their scores on the Brief Resilience Scale (BRS; Smith et al. 2008), with applicants scoring greater than 4.3 out of 5 being excluded in order to decrease the likelihood of a ceiling effect.
text.formatted: Participants were selected based on their scores on the Brief Resilience Scale (BRS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Smith et al. 2008)</ref>, with applicants scoring greater than 4.3 out of 5 being excluded in order to decrease the likelihood of a ceiling effect.

text.text: From a total of 151 participants who completed an initial pre-training survey, 7 were excluded due to a BRS score greater than 4.3, and 144 were invited to participate in the study, of which 121 accepted.
Of those 121, 23 voluntarily dropped out during the intervention or control stage, leading to a final RCT sample of 98 participants providing self-report data at pre-training and post-training.
Participants were randomly allocated to either Stoic Training (pre-training n = 61, post-training n = 46) or Active Control (pre-training n = 60, post-training n = 52).

Groups did not significantly vary on age, biological sex, gender, first generation student status, subjective social status, or race/ethnicity (see Supplement for details) nor did they vary on any pre-training self-report measures (see Table 2).
text.formatted: Groups did not significantly vary on age, biological sex, gender, first generation student status, subjective social status, or race/ethnicity (see Supplement for details) nor did they vary on any pre-training self-report measures (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: However, pre-training subjective social status relative to the country as a whole (p = .061) and first-generation status (p = .072) were trending towards significance (see Supplement).
All 98 participants who completed the post-training survey were invited to participate in a lab visit, of whom 78 completed a lab visit (n = 39 Stoic, n = 39 Control).

For our preregistered analyses of heart rate (HR) and heart rate variability (HRV), usable electrocardiography (ECG) data were available for 66 of the 78 participants who visited the lab (84.6%; n = 32 Stoic, n = 34 Control).
For phase-specific exploratory analyses, usable data were available for 65-69 participants (83.3%-88.5%; see Supplement for details).
For STAI-S and SUDS, data were available for all 78 participants who completed the lab visit.
Participants first completed an online survey containing self-report questionnaires and demographic information.
Participants who met eligibility criteria were then randomized to either the Stoic or Control condition and sent an online access link for their assigned condition.
Participants were not informed that the study involved multiple experimental conditions or that they were receiving an intervention.
Instead, they were told that the study examined associations between responses to daily writing prompts, stress reactivity, and resilience.
The full study design was disclosed during debriefing after completion of the laboratory session.
The mean number of training days participants took to complete the eight sessions of Stoic training was 11.39 days, SD = 3.16, with the median number of days being 11.
After completing the training period, participants completed the same self-report questionnaires administered at baseline.
Participants were then invited to schedule a laboratory visit and were encouraged to attend within four calendar days of completing their assigned training or control activities.
When scheduling within this window was not feasible, later visits were permitted to maximize participant retention.
The mean interval between completion of the assigned activities and the laboratory visit was 3.82 calendar days (median = 3, range = 1-21).
Of the 82 laboratory attendees, 23 (28.0%) attended more than four calendar days after completion.

Accordingly, sensitivity analyses repeated the preregistered laboratory outcome models with the number of calendar days between completion and the laboratory visit included as an additional covariate.
Prior to the lab visit, participants were asked to refrain from caffeine for 6 hours, alcohol for 12 hours, and food and vigorous exercise for 3 hours.
During the lab visit, participants completed brief pre-task questionnaires to measure adherence to protocol and baseline state anxiety.
After completing self-report forms, participants were connected to physiological recording equipment, completed a modified TSST, and self-reported post-TSST state anxiety.

Pre-task questionnaires revealed that one participant reported caffeine consumption within 6 hours of their lab visit and one reported vigorous exercise within 3 hours of their lab visit; no participants reported food consumption within 3 hours or alcohol consumption within 12 hours.
Sensitivity analyses were run to account for deviations from protocol.
The Stoic training was delivered online following procedures established in MacLellan & Derakshan (2021).
text.formatted: The Stoic training was delivered online following procedures established in <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">MacLellan & Derakshan (2021)</ref>.

text.text: Briefly, participants in the Stoic condition completed 8 daily training sessions.
Participants were instructed to complete the eight sessions within 12 days, although additional time was permitted when necessary.

The 8 daily sessions consisted of three recurring daily activities: Negative Visualization, Stoic Mindfulness, and Stoic Reflection; participants in the Stoic condition also read and summarized a daily Stoic reading for each of the 8 days.
The daily reading changed each day and included passages of Stoic text followed by instructions to summarize their thoughts about the passages.
By contrast, the active control entailed reading literary fiction passages followed by instructions to summarize and reflect on those passages.
All training materials were delivered via Qualtrics and the full Stoic training and active control materials can be found in the Supplement.

Participants completed the Stoic Attitudes and Behaviours Scale to measure Stoicism as a life philosophy (SABS; LeBon et al., 2026), Brief Fear of Negative Evaluation Scale to measure fear of negative evaluation (BFNE; Leary 1983), the Ruminative Response Scale-10 to measure rumination (RRS-10; Treynor et al., 2003), the General Self-Efficacy Scale to measure selfefficacy (GSE; Schwarzer & Jerusalem 1995), the Brief Resilience Scale to measure resilience as the ability to bounce back from stress (BRS; Smith et al. 2008), and the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale-10 to measure resilience as perceived ability to cope with and adapt to adversity (CD-RISC-10; Campbell-Sills and Stein 2007).

text.text: Participants completed a modified version of the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST; Kirschbaum et al., 1993), a standardized laboratory stressor designed to elicit social-evaluative threat.
text.formatted: Participants completed a modified version of the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST; <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Kirschbaum et al., 1993)</ref>, a standardized laboratory stressor designed to elicit social-evaluative threat.

text.text: The task followed standard TSST procedures with one additional phase: a 5-minute intervention/control phase was added immediately before speech preparation.

During this phase, participants assigned to Stoic training were instructed to apply the practice of Negative Visualization to the upcoming social stress task during a 5-minute period, whereas participants assigned to the control condition were instructed to wait quietly for 5 minutes.

The full task sequence consisted of a 5-minute seated baseline, 5-minute intervention/control phase, 5minute speech preparation period, 5-minute speech, 5-minute mental arithmetic task, and 5minute recovery period.
For the speech task, participants were instructed to give a speech about why they were qualified for their dream job in front of two evaluative panelists.
For the mental arithmetic task, participants were instructed to serially subtract 13 from 1,022 as quickly and accurately as possible and to start over if they made an error.
Physiological measures were recorded continuously throughout the task.
Participants remained seated throughout the procedure and were instructed to remain as still as possible during physiological recording.
TSST panelists were aware of condition assignment because the laboratory procedure included a condition-specific intervention/control phase immediately before speech preparation.
The full standardized TSST script can be found in the Supplement.
Electrocardiography (ECG) was recorded continuously using a Biopac MP36R data acquisition system (Biopac Systems, Inc., Goleta, CA).

ECG was recorded from three Ag/AgCl electrodes; one electrode was placed below the right clavicle in the second intercostal space, and one electrode was placed on each lower rib cage in the eighth intercostal space.
ECG data were acquired at a sampling rate of 1,000 Hz, amplified, and digitized using the Biopac MP36R system.
Electrodes were also placed on the palms to record galvanic skin response (GSR).

However, for GSR, frequent electrode detachment resulted in unreliable signal quality, and no standardized procedure was available to determine consistently which participants had provided usable recordings.
GSR data were therefore not processed or analyzed.
Although blood pressure was included in the preregistered protocol, it was removed before data collection because equipment failure prevented its acquisition.
ECG data were segmented into six 5-min phases: baseline, intervention/control, speech preparation, speech, mental arithmetic, and recovery.
ECG data were processed and screened prior to hypothesis testing and blind to participant condition.
ECG data were high-pass filtered at 3 Hz and low-pass filtered at 35 Hz.

The 3-Hz lower cutoff was consistent with prior ECG preprocessing in TSST research before QRS detection and RR-interval calculation (Ringgold et al., 2025), while low-pass cutoffs of approximately 35-40 Hz have been commonly used in ECG preprocessing (e.g., Tejedor et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The 3-Hz lower cutoff was consistent with prior ECG preprocessing in TSST research before QRS detection and RR-interval calculation <ref type="bibr">(Ringgold et al., 2025)</ref>, while low-pass cutoffs of approximately 35-40 Hz have been commonly used in ECG preprocessing (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Tejedor et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: R-peaks were identified in AcqKnowledge and were visually inspected for signal quality.
Segments with recording failures or unusable signal quality were removed following visual inspection.
Continuous RR interval data and event markers were exported for further processing.
In R, RR intervals were flagged as invalid if they were physiologically implausible (<0.30 s or >2.00 s) or deviated by more than 30% from an 11-beat rolling median.
text.formatted: In R, RR intervals were flagged as invalid if they were physiologically implausible (<0.30 s or >2.00 s) or deviated by more than 30% from an 11-beat rolling median.

text.text: Flagged RR intervals were visually inspected and then set to missing.
Five-minute segments were treated as missing when 10% or more of RR intervals within that segment were invalid.

Applying these criteria, usable HR and HRV data were available for 69 participants during baseline, intervention/control, speech preparation, and speech; 66 participants during mental arithmetic; and 65 participants during recovery.
HR was calculated as 60 divided by the mean RR interval within each phase.

HRV was operationalized as the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD), calculated from RR intervals within each 5-min phase and natural-log transformed prior to analysis (Laborde et al., 2017).
text.formatted: HRV was operationalized as the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD), calculated from RR intervals within each 5-min phase and natural-log transformed prior to analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Laborde et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: State anxiety was assessed using the state subscale of the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-S; Spielberger et al., 1983).
text.formatted: State anxiety was assessed using the state subscale of the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-S; <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Spielberger et al., 1983)</ref>.

text.text: The STAI-S was administered immediately before and after the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) to assess changes in state anxiety associated with the stressor.
Momentary subjective distress was assessed using the Subjective Units of Distress Scale (SUDS; Wolpe, 1969).
text.formatted: Momentary subjective distress was assessed using the Subjective Units of Distress Scale (SUDS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Wolpe, 1969)</ref>.

text.text: Participants rated their current level of distress on a scale ranging from 0 (no distress at all) to 100 (the most distress imaginable), with higher ratings indicating greater subjective distress.
SUDS ratings were obtained at the following 6 timepoints: prior to baseline, after baseline, after intervention/control, after speech preparation, after TSST, after recovery.
All analyses were performed in R (R Core Team, 2026).
Unless otherwise specified, tests were two-tailed with α = .05.
To evaluate whether the modified TSST successfully elicited stressrelated changes, we conducted manipulation-check models comparing HR, HRV, and SUDS across baseline, TSST, and recovery.
For HR and HRV, TSST values were averaged across the speech and mental-arithmetic phases.

Manipulation checks were conducted using linear mixed-effects models estimated with the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015), with phase entered as a within-participant fixed effect and a random intercept for participant.
text.formatted: Manipulation checks were conducted using linear mixed-effects models estimated with the lme4 package <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bates et al., 2015)</ref>, with phase entered as a within-participant fixed effect and a random intercept for participant.

text.text: Primary preregistered hypotheses were tested using linear regression models with group assignment as the predictor of interest and baseline levels of the outcome measure included as a covariate.

Thus, for preregistered self-report outcomes, separate models tested Stoic training effects on post-treatment FNE, rumination, self-efficacy, and resilience while controlling for the corresponding pretreatment score.

SABS was analyzed using an analogous baseline-adjusted regression model with post-treatment SABS as the dependent variable, group assignment as the predictor of interest, and baseline SABS as a covariate.
For preregistered TSST outcomes, separate models tested Stoic training effects on HR, HRV, and SUDS while controlling for the corresponding baseline score.
The TSST-average physiology variables were computed from the speech and mental-arithmetic phases and required valid data from both phases.
State anxiety was examined using the preregistered one-tailed independent-samples t test, with change in STAI-S from pre-to post-TSST compared between conditions.
For regression models, adjusted standardized mean differences were calculated by dividing the condition coefficient by the model residual standard deviation (Hedges et al., 2023).
text.formatted: For regression models, adjusted standardized mean differences were calculated by dividing the condition coefficient by the model residual standard deviation <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hedges et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For STAI-S, Cohen's d represented the standardized between-condition difference in change scores.
Preregistered GSR and blood-pressure analyses were not conducted because bloodpressure equipment failure prevented data collection and GSR signal quality could not be evaluated reliably.
Exploratory analyses were conducted to characterize SABS subscales, within-group change in self-report outcomes, and the time course of physiological effects.
Paired-samples t tests examined pre-to post-treatment change separately within the Stoic and control groups for each self-report outcome.
Following the same analytic approach used for the preregistered selfreport analyses, analogous exploratory baseline-adjusted regression models tested Stoic training effects on SABS subscales.
Exploratory linear regressions also tested condition differences in baseline HR and HRV.

To clarify the phase-specific pattern of physiological effects, separate baseline-adjusted regressions tested Stoic training effects on HR and HRV during the intervention/control, speech-preparation, speech, mental-arithmetic, and recovery phases.
In addition, exploratory linear mixed-effects models included the fixed effects of condition, phase, and their interaction, with participant included as a random intercept.
Follow-up contrasts, estimated using the emmeans package (Lenth & Piaskowski, 2026), tested group differences at each phase and whether baseline-relative changes differed by condition.
text.formatted: Follow-up contrasts, estimated using the emmeans package <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Lenth & Piaskowski, 2026)</ref>, tested group differences at each phase and whether baseline-relative changes differed by condition.

text.text: Phase-specific regressions included participants with valid baseline and outcome data for the relevant phase, whereas mixed-effects models used all available valid phase-level observations.
To control the familywise error rate, Hommel adjustments were applied separately within prespecified families of exploratory tests (Hommel, 1988).
text.formatted: To control the familywise error rate, Hommel adjustments were applied separately within prespecified families of exploratory tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Hommel, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: The within-condition pre-to posttreatment comparisons formed one family within the Stoic condition and one family within the control condition.
All seven SABS subscale regression models formed one family.
The phasespecific regression models formed separate families for HR, HRV, and SUDS, with the postbaseline phases corrected within each outcome.
Follow-up between-condition comparisons derived from the mixed-effects models also formed separate families for HR, HRV, and SUDS.
Prior to hypothesis testing, we examined baseline differences between the Stoic training and control groups on pre-treatment self-report outcomes and demographics.
In cases of significant differences or meeting our prespecified p < .1 sensitivity analysis criterion, we conducted sensitivity analyses with those variables included as covariates.
text.formatted: In cases of significant differences or meeting our prespecified p < .1 sensitivity analysis criterion, we conducted sensitivity analyses with those variables included as covariates.

text.text: Thus, for self-report outcomes, sensitivity analyses were performed by repeating pre-registered regression analyses with the addition of subjective social status relative to the country as a covariate and then separately with first generation status as a covariate.
For TSST outcomes, we repeated preregistered regression analyses with the addition of subjective social status relative to the country as a covariate.
Additional sensitivity analyses evaluated laboratory timing and deviations from the intended laboratory protocol.

Participants were encouraged to attend the laboratory visit within four calendar days of completing their assigned training or control activities, although later visits were permitted when scheduling within this window was not feasible.

To evaluate whether variability in visit timing affected the findings, the preregistered TSST outcome models were repeated with the number of calendar days between completion of the assigned activities and the laboratory visit included as an additional covariate.

In a separate protocol-adherence analysis, the preregistered TSST models were repeated after excluding two participants: one who reported consuming caffeine within six hours of the laboratory visit and one who reported engaging in vigorous exercise within three hours of the laboratory visit.
Missingness was evaluated separately for self-report outcomes and TSST outcomes.
Attrition for post-training self-report outcomes was evaluated among participants with identifiable Day 1 training data.

We examined whether completion of the intervention and subsequent post-training assessment differed by condition and whether it was associated with baseline SABS, FNE, CD-RISC, BRS, GSE, or RRS scores.

To evaluate the robustness of the preregistered self-report outcome findings to missing data, the baseline-adjusted models were repeated using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE; van Buuren & Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011).

In support of preregistered Hypothesis 1a, Stoic training was associated with lower posttraining fear of negative evaluation after adjustment for pretraining BFNE scores, b = -2.77, SE = 1.13, t(95) = -2.45, p = .016, 95% CI [-5.01, -0.53], adjusted d = -0.50.

Consistent with this effect, BFNE scores decreased within the Stoic training condition from pre-to posttraining, mean change = -2.76, 95% CI [-4.57, -0.95], p = .004, Hommel-adjusted p = .012, whereas the control condition showed no significant change, mean change = -0.19, 95% CI [-1.61, 1.22], p = .786.
Contrary to preregistered Hypothesis 1b, Stoic training was not associated with lower subjective distress during the TSST.

After adjustment for baseline SUDS, participants assigned to Stoic training reported numerically higher SUDS during the TSST, but the condition effect was not statistically significant, b = 3.77, SE = 3.56, t(76) = 1.06, p = .293, 95% CI [-3.33, 10.87], adjusted d = 0.24.
The preregistered analysis of state anxiety also did not support the hypothesized effect.

Although the mean increase in STAI-S scores from before to after the TSST was smaller in the Stoic training condition (2.65 points) than in the control condition (5.41 points), the preregistered onetailed Welch's t test did not indicate a significant between-condition difference, t(63.92) = 1.24, p = .109, adjusted d = -.29.

Contrary to preregistered Hypothesis 1c, Stoic training was associated with higher rather than lower heart rate during the TSST after adjustment for baseline heart rate, b = 4.13, SE = 1.95, t(63) = 2.12, p = .038, 95% CI [0.24, 8.02], adjusted d = 0.53.
Contrary to preregistered Hypothesis 1d, the estimated effect on heart-rate variability was also opposite to the hypothesized direction.

After adjustment for baseline HRV, Stoic training was associated with lower HRV during the TSST, although the effect narrowly missed the preregistered threshold for statistical significance, b = -0.17, SE = 0.08, t(63) = -1.97, p = .053, 95% CI [-0.335, 0.002], adjusted d = -0.49.
Thus, Stoic training was associated with lower broad FNE, but it did not produce the hypothesized attenuation of subjective or cardiac responses to acute social evaluation.

Sensitivity analyses adjusting separately for first-generation status and subjective social status relative to the United States produced effects that were consistent in direction and generally consistent in magnitude with the preregistered models.
All findings that were statistically significant in the primary analyses remained significant after covariate adjustment.
The estimated HRV effect, which narrowly missed significance in the primary model, reached statistical significance after adjustment for subjective social status, p = .043.
When excluding the two participants who reported deviations from laboratory preparation requirements, the HR effect remained significant and the HRV effect reached statistical significance, p = .043.

Adjustment for the interval between training completion and the laboratory visit also did not meaningfully alter the TSST findings: the HR effect remained significant, p = .045, the HRV effect remained similar in magnitude but nonsignificant, p = .062, and the interval itself was unrelated to the laboratory outcomes, all ps ≥ .360.
Posttraining completion did not differ significantly by condition, and no baseline self-report variable was significantly associated with completion after correction for multiple comparisons.
In multiple-imputation analyses, the estimated effect of Stoic training on FNE remained statistically significant.

The estimated effect of Stoic training on SABS remained positive and similar in magnitude to the complete-case estimate but was no longer statistically significant in the primary imputed analysis, p = .075, indicating that inference regarding SABS target engagement was somewhat sensitive to the treatment of missing posttraining data.
Physiological and laboratory self-report missingness was limited, compatible with data missing completely at random, and unrelated to condition.
HR and HRV findings were also robust when TSST averages were calculated using whichever of the speech and mental-arithmetic phases was available.
Under this specification, the effect of Stoic training on HR remained significant, p = .027, and the effect on HRV reached statistical significance, p = .022.

The present study examined whether a brief, digitally delivered Stoic training intervention could reduce FNE, alter broader psychological outcomes, increase Stoic attitudes and behaviors, and influence subjective and cardiac responses to acute social-evaluative stress.

Stoic training was associated with a moderate reduction in broad FNE relative to an active control, and this effect remained evident across sensitivity analyses addressing baseline characteristics and missing posttraining data.

To our knowledge, this is the first RCT to demonstrate that a digitally delivered intervention can produce a significantly greater reduction in broad FNE than an active control among college students when administered during an ongoing academic semester.
Stoic training was also associated with higher posttraining SABS scores in the complete-case analysis.

To our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate a significant between-condition increase in the attitudes and behaviors targeted by Stoic training, although this finding was less robust to the treatment of missing data.
By contrast, betweencondition differences in resilience, self-efficacy, and rumination were not statistically significant.
Finally, the laboratory findings did not support the hypothesis that Stoic training would attenuate acute social-evaluative stress responses.

Cardiac effects were instead opposite to prediction, with Stoic training associated with higher HR and lower HRV during the TSST, whereas subjective distress and state-anxiety responses did not differ significantly between conditions.

Together, these findings suggest that brief Stoic training may reduce broad FNE and increase Stoic attitudes and behaviors, while effects on the other psychological outcomes assessed here were more limited and cardiac responses to acute social-evaluative stress were amplified rather than attenuated.

The reduction in FNE is particularly notable given the limited evidence that brief or scalable interventions reduce broad FNE relative to active comparison conditions in college populations (Hoppitt et al., 2014; Zaboski et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The reduction in FNE is particularly notable given the limited evidence that brief or scalable interventions reduce broad FNE relative to active comparison conditions in college populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Hoppitt et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zaboski et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings extend prior work by showing that a brief, digitally delivered intervention can produce a between-condition reduction in broad FNE, when compared to an active control, while students are already navigating ongoing academic and interpersonal demands.

This complements earlier evidence from interventions delivered before or around the transition to college (Hoppitt et al., 2014), while also addressing a more ecologically typical period in which social-evaluative concerns are already embedded in day-to-day academic and social life (Campbell et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This complements earlier evidence from interventions delivered before or around the transition to college <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Hoppitt et al., 2014)</ref>, while also addressing a more ecologically typical period in which social-evaluative concerns are already embedded in day-to-day academic and social life <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Campbell et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: More broadly, the findings add to evidence that FNE may be modifiable through relatively brief cognitive interventions (Arai et al., 2023; Hoppitt et al., 2014; McCall et al., 2018), while suggesting that a broad philosophical training approach can influence this vulnerability even when it is not designed as a disorder-specific treatment.
text.formatted: More broadly, the findings add to evidence that FNE may be modifiable through relatively brief cognitive interventions <ref type="bibr">(Arai et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Hoppitt et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">McCall et al., 2018)</ref>, while suggesting that a broad philosophical training approach can influence this vulnerability even when it is not designed as a disorder-specific treatment.

text.text: The FNE finding is consistent with the possibility that Stoic training may have altered appraisals that are especially relevant to social evaluation.

In particular, the intervention may have reduced the perceived importance or intolerability of others' judgments, or increased confidence in coping with unfavorable evaluation, consistent with cognitive models emphasizing maladaptive beliefs about social evaluation and its consequences (Clark & Wells, 1995; Hofmann, 2007; Rapee & Heimberg, 1997).
text.formatted: In particular, the intervention may have reduced the perceived importance or intolerability of others' judgments, or increased confidence in coping with unfavorable evaluation, consistent with cognitive models emphasizing maladaptive beliefs about social evaluation and its consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clark & Wells, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Hofmann, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rapee & Heimberg, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: This interpretation is supported indirectly by the concurrent increase in total SABS scores in the primary complete-case analysis, suggesting that reductions in FNE occurred alongside greater endorsement of the Stoic attitudes and behaviors targeted by the intervention.

At the same time, the present study did not test, nor was designed with sufficient timepoints and statistical power to test, whether changes in SABS mediated the FNE effect, and the reduction in FNE cannot be attributed to any specific Stoic facet or practice.

Future work should employ longitudinal designs with three or more measurement occasions to establish temporal ordering (Maxwell & Cole, 2007) and test whether changes in Stoic attitudes, perceived controllability, catastrophic beliefs about social evaluation, coping confidence, anticipatory processing, or impression-management efforts mediate subsequent reductions in FNE.
text.formatted: Future work should employ longitudinal designs with three or more measurement occasions to establish temporal ordering <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Maxwell & Cole, 2007)</ref> and test whether changes in Stoic attitudes, perceived controllability, catastrophic beliefs about social evaluation, coping confidence, anticipatory processing, or impression-management efforts mediate subsequent reductions in FNE.

text.text: The increase in total SABS scores is also important given the growing interest in Stoic training as a psychological intervention and emerging evidence that the attitudes and behaviors captured by the SABS are meaningfully associated with mental health and well-being.

Higher SABS scores have recently been linked cross-sectionally with greater well-being, resilience, selfefficacy, character strengths, and cognitive reappraisal, as well as lower worry, dysfunctional attitudes, emotion-regulation difficulties, and dysfunctional anger (Karl & LeBon, 2026; LeBon et al., 2026; MacLellan & Lewis, 2026), suggesting that Stoic attitudes may represent a potentially meaningful intervention target rather than merely a marker of philosophical identification.
text.formatted: Higher SABS scores have recently been linked cross-sectionally with greater well-being, resilience, selfefficacy, character strengths, and cognitive reappraisal, as well as lower worry, dysfunctional attitudes, emotion-regulation difficulties, and dysfunctional anger <ref type="bibr">(Karl & LeBon, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">LeBon et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">MacLellan & Lewis, 2026)</ref>, suggesting that Stoic attitudes may represent a potentially meaningful intervention target rather than merely a marker of philosophical identification.

text.text: Against this background, the present between-condition effect is notable because prior intervention studies have provided only within-group evidence of change in Stoic attitudes or have failed to detect a significant controlled effect (Brown et al., 2022; MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021).
text.formatted: Against this background, the present between-condition effect is notable because prior intervention studies have provided only within-group evidence of change in Stoic attitudes or have failed to detect a significant controlled effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brown et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: To our knowledge, the present study therefore provides the first RCT evidence that Stoic training can produce a significant increase in SABS scores relative to a control condition.

This finding provides preliminary support for the malleability of Stoic attitudes under experimental conditions and strengthens the rationale for treating SABS as an intervention target in future Stoic training research.

At the same time, the effect should be interpreted cautiously: although its direction and approximate magnitude were similar under multiple imputation, it no longer reached statistical significance when missing posttraining data were imputed.
Replication in larger samples will therefore be important for establishing the robustness of the betweencondition effect.
Exploratory analyses further suggested that some dimensions of Stoic attitudes may be more responsive to brief training than others.

To our knowledge, this is also the first study to examine intervention-related change across individual SABS subscales, providing an initial indication of which facets of Stoic attitudes may be most malleable under brief training.

Baseline-adjusted between-condition effects were nominally significant for Beliefs About Happiness and Beliefs About Control, although neither remained significant following correction for multiple comparisons.
Within the Stoic condition, Beliefs About Control and Stoic Worldview increased and were significant after correction, with a smaller uncorrected increase in Stoic Mindfulness.
These exploratory findings should be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than evidence that Stoic training selectively changes particular SABS facets.
They are also necessarily specific to the content of the present intervention and the population studied.
Other forms of Stoic training may place greater emphasis on different philosophical principles and may therefore produce different profiles of change across SABS dimensions.

Future research could examine whether particular intervention components preferentially target specific SABS facets and whether those facets, in turn, are differentially associated with particular psychological outcomes or populations.

Such work could eventually inform more targeted or personalized Stoic interventions, in which training components are selected according to the attitudes most relevant to a given psychological vulnerability, population, or intervention goal.

In the present study, Beliefs About Control and Beliefs About Happiness may warrant particular attention because both are theoretically relevant to FNE: Stoic beliefs about control emphasize directing effort toward one's own actions rather than other people's evaluations, whereas Stoic beliefs about happiness challenge the assumption that reputation or social approval is necessary for well-being (Clark & Wells, 1995; LeBon et al., 2026; Rapee & Heimberg, 1997).
text.formatted: In the present study, Beliefs About Control and Beliefs About Happiness may warrant particular attention because both are theoretically relevant to FNE: Stoic beliefs about control emphasize directing effort toward one's own actions rather than other people's evaluations, whereas Stoic beliefs about happiness challenge the assumption that reputation or social approval is necessary for well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clark & Wells, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">LeBon et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Rapee & Heimberg, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Larger longitudinal trials could determine whether changes in these facets reliably occur following training and whether they mediate reductions in FNE or other psychological outcomes.
In contrast to the FNE findings, the preregistered hypotheses concerning self-efficacy, rumination, and resilience were not supported.

For self-efficacy and rumination, the present findings did not replicate the previously reported between-condition improvements following Stoic training (MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021), underscoring the need for additional studies to establish potential boundary conditions.
text.formatted: For self-efficacy and rumination, the present findings did not replicate the previously reported between-condition improvements following Stoic training <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(MacLellan & Derakshan, 2021)</ref>, underscoring the need for additional studies to establish potential boundary conditions.

text.text: Of note, MacLellan and Derakshan (2021) recruited individuals selected for high worry from a university and surrounding community, whereas the present study involved a general undergraduate sample, potentially leaving less scope for improvement on some outcomes.
Regarding resilience, Brown et al. (2022) previously reported a within-group increase in resilience as measured using the BRS among medical students receiving Stoic training.
text.formatted: Regarding resilience, <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Brown et al. (2022)</ref> previously reported a within-group increase in resilience as measured using the BRS among medical students receiving Stoic training.

text.text: Consistent with that finding, the present study found significant increases in resilience as measured by the BRS and CD-RISC within the Stoic training group, both of which survived correction for multiple comparisons.
However, the present study extends that earlier work by including an active control and found no significant between-condition effect on either resilience measure.
This distinction highlights the importance of separating pre-to-post improvement within an intervention group from evidence that change exceeds what occurs under a comparison condition.

Taken as a whole, our findings are consistent with the possibility that FNE may represent a comparatively proximal target of the particular Stoic principles emphasized in the present intervention, whereas resilience, general self-efficacy, and rumination are broader constructs that may require greater intervention exposure, specific target populations, and/or additional opportunities to apply Stoic practices across contexts.
At the same time, the present null findings should not be interpreted as demonstrating that Stoic training has no effect on these constructs.

Rather, this study did not provide evidence that the present brief intervention produced detectable between-condition changes in these broader outcomes, measured immediately post-training, in this sample.

Replication across larger and more diverse samples, longer training periods, and follow-up assessments will be important for determining the breadth and durability of psychological change following Stoic training.
The laboratory findings provide a different and more complex picture.
To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine physiological responses to acute stress following a Stoic intervention.

Contrary to prediction, participants assigned to Stoic training exhibited higher baseline-adjusted HR during the TSST and lower baseline-adjusted HRV, although the preregistered HRV effect narrowly missed the conventional significance threshold.

Exploratory time-course analyses further indicated greater baseline-to-speech increases in HR and decreases in HRV among participants in the Stoic condition, with both contrasts remaining significant after correction for multiple comparisons.

Notably, the conditions did not differ in baseline HR or HRV, indicating that the cardiac divergence emerged during the subsequent laboratory challenge rather than reflecting pre-existing differences at the start of the session.
These findings do not support the hypothesis that Stoic training attenuates cardiac mobilization during social-evaluative stress.
Importantly, however, the greater cardiac response was not accompanied by significantly greater subjective distress or state-anxiety responding.
The physiological findings therefore should not be interpreted as evidence of a straightforward increase in experienced distress.
Several interpretations of this pattern remain possible.

Although higher HR and lower HRV are characteristic of acute stress responding, neither response has a uniquely negative psychological meaning, and cardiac autonomic activity should not be reduced to a simple continuum from parasympathetic "calm" to sympathetic "stress" (Berntson et al., 1993 (Berntson et al., , 1997)).
text.formatted: Although higher HR and lower HRV are characteristic of acute stress responding, neither response has a uniquely negative psychological meaning, and cardiac autonomic activity should not be reduced to a simple continuum from parasympathetic "calm" to sympathetic "stress" <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Berntson et al., 1993</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Berntson et al., , 1997))</ref>.

text.text: Depending on context, elevated HR and lower HRV during acute stress may be either adaptive or maladaptive (e.g., Laborde et al., 2017; Seery, 2011).
text.formatted: Depending on context, elevated HR and lower HRV during acute stress may be either adaptive or maladaptive (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Laborde et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Seery, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Greater HR activation and vagal withdrawal could reflect heightened threat or stress responding, but they could also accompany greater effort mobilization, task engagement, or regulatory demand during a challenging performance (Blascovich & Mendes, 2010; Seery, 2011).
text.formatted: Greater HR activation and vagal withdrawal could reflect heightened threat or stress responding, but they could also accompany greater effort mobilization, task engagement, or regulatory demand during a challenging performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Blascovich & Mendes, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Seery, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, one possibility is that applying Negative Visualization immediately before the TSST increased the salience of possible failure or negative evaluation, temporarily increasing anticipatory mobilization even if repeated Stoic practice had reduced broader beliefs about the consequences of unfavorable evaluation.

This interpretation would be consistent with evidence that contemplating potential negative outcomes can sometimes increase anticipatory arousal (Makkar & Grisham, 2011; Schulz et al., 2008), an effect that may be particularly likely when individuals have had limited time to consolidate the broader Stoic framework.
text.formatted: This interpretation would be consistent with evidence that contemplating potential negative outcomes can sometimes increase anticipatory arousal <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Makkar & Grisham, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Schulz et al., 2008)</ref>, an effect that may be particularly likely when individuals have had limited time to consolidate the broader Stoic framework.

text.text: In this sense, Negative Visualization may initially have produced a paradoxical effect opposite to its intended regulatory function.

Analogous responses have been documented during relaxation-based practices, in which attempts to reduce arousal can paradoxically increase anxiety in some individuals (Heide & Borkovec, 1984; Kim & Newman, 2019).
text.formatted: Analogous responses have been documented during relaxation-based practices, in which attempts to reduce arousal can paradoxically increase anxiety in some individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Heide & Borkovec, 1984;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kim & Newman, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, Stoic training participants may have engaged more actively with the performance task or exerted greater regulatory effort without experiencing correspondingly greater subjective distress.
From this perspective, greater acute cardiac activation need not indicate a detrimental response and could instead accompany more active engagement with a challenging experience.

Consistent with this interpretation, greater HR reactivity to acute psychological stress has prospectively predicted better subsequent academic performance, suggesting that larger cardiac responses can accompany adaptive engagement or performance rather than distress alone (Ginty et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Consistent with this interpretation, greater HR reactivity to acute psychological stress has prospectively predicted better subsequent academic performance, suggesting that larger cardiac responses can accompany adaptive engagement or performance rather than distress alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Ginty et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This possibility is also broadly consistent with exposure-based models in which therapeutic benefit does not require low levels of distress during the challenging experience itself but may emerge through sustained engagement and new learning in the presence of distress (Craske et al., 2014; Rupp et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This possibility is also broadly consistent with exposure-based models in which therapeutic benefit does not require low levels of distress during the challenging experience itself but may emerge through sustained engagement and new learning in the presence of distress <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Craske et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Rupp et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, the present measures cannot distinguish among these possibilities, and the dissociation between cardiac and subjective responses underscores that greater physiological activation should not be interpreted in isolation as evidence of a more adverse stress response.

Future work incorporating broader cardiovascular indices, ideally incorporating measures such as Total Peripheral Resistance to distinguish threat from challenge (Seery, 2011), alongside additional subjective and behavioral measures, will be needed to determine whether the observed pattern reflects heightened threat, greater task engagement, increased regulatory effort, or some combination of these processes.
text.formatted: Future work incorporating broader cardiovascular indices, ideally incorporating measures such as Total Peripheral Resistance to distinguish threat from challenge <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Seery, 2011)</ref>, alongside additional subjective and behavioral measures, will be needed to determine whether the observed pattern reflects heightened threat, greater task engagement, increased regulatory effort, or some combination of these processes.

text.text: The recovery-period findings also warrant attention.

In the exploratory phase-specific baseline-adjusted regression analyses, lower HRV in the Stoic condition remained evident during recovery, and this was the only phase-specific cardiac difference to remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons.

Although this finding should be interpreted cautiously, the persistence of lower HRV after the active stressor had ended is more consistent with sustained autonomic activation or slower vagal recovery than with an effect limited to transient task engagement during the speech itself.
This pattern is therefore consistent with the possibility that Negative Visualization had a paradoxical stress-enhancing effect in this sample of novice Stoic practitioners.

At the same time, the present design cannot determine whether the recovery pattern reflects a more prolonged threat response or lingering autonomic activation associated with greater engagement during the preceding task.
Future studies should examine recovery slope more directly using a longer recovery period and repeated post-stressor assessments.

A critical limitation of the laboratory design is that the effects of the broader Stoic intervention cannot be separated from those of the acute Negative Visualization exercise administered immediately before speech preparation.

The acute exercise was included to increase sensitivity to potential intervention-related differences in stress responding by reactivating a core Stoic practice immediately before the social-evaluative challenge, particularly given the absence of a pretreatment laboratory stress assessment.
However, this design choice also complicates interpretation of the resulting condition differences.

Participants in the Stoic condition had completed eight sessions of internet-delivered Stoic training and then engaged in five minutes of Negative Visualization immediately before receiving the speech instructions, whereas control participants completed eight sessions of the active control and spent the corresponding five-minute period waiting quietly.

Consequently, the greater cardiac response could reflect the cumulative effects of Stoic training, the immediate effects of Negative Visualization, differences produced by the contrasting pre-stressor activities themselves, or an interaction among these factors.

In particular, the quiet waiting period may have afforded control participants additional physiological acclimatization or settling immediately before the stressor, whereas Negative Visualization may have maintained or increased anticipatory activation (Hastrup, 1986; Laborde et al., 2017).
text.formatted: In particular, the quiet waiting period may have afforded control participants additional physiological acclimatization or settling immediately before the stressor, whereas Negative Visualization may have maintained or increased anticipatory activation <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Hastrup, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Laborde et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies should experimentally separate the repeated and acute components, for example using a factorial design in which prior Stoic training and immediate pre-stressor Negative Visualization are independently manipulated.

Such a design could determine whether repeated training alters acute stress responding, whether immediate Negative Visualization has distinct effects among trained and untrained individuals, and whether the timing of Negative Visualization influences its consequences.
Beyond the laboratory design considerations discussed above, several additional limitations should be considered alongside the study's methodological strengths.

The study used a preregistered randomized design with an active comparison condition and a substantially larger sample than prior peer-reviewed evaluations of Stoic training, providing greater precision for estimating between-condition effects.

It also assessed both intervention outcomes and target engagement, incorporated subjective and physiological measures of acute social-evaluative responding, and made study materials, analysis code, and deidentified data openly available.
Sensitivity analyses further indicated that the principal FNE finding was robust to adjustment for baseline characteristics and to multiple imputation for missing posttraining data.

The focus on undergraduates was also a strength insofar as college students are a population of particular relevance to the mental health concerns motivating the study; however, the single-college, predominantly female sample limits generalizability to students at other institutions and to nonstudent adults.

Attrition occurred between enrollment and posttraining assessment, and although completion did not differ significantly by condition and the FNE effect remained significant following multiple imputation, missing data introduce additional uncertainty.

The inlab sample was smaller than the self-report sample, limiting precision for TSST measures, and the absence of a pretreatment laboratory stress assessment prevented examination of intervention-related change in stress reactivity from before to after training.
Although there was some variability in the training-to-laboratory interval, the interval was not associated with the laboratory outcomes, and adjusting for it did not meaningfully alter the findings.
The intervention also did not directly assess the cognitive processes hypothesized to account for reductions in FNE, precluding conclusions regarding mechanism or mediation.

Finally, outcomes were assessed only immediately following training, leaving unclear whether reductions in FNE and changes in Stoic attitudes persist or translate into behavioral and functional improvements over time.
Replication in larger and more diverse samples, with longer-term follow-up and more direct assessment of hypothesized mechanisms, will therefore be important.

Overall, the present findings provide initial evidence that a brief, digitally delivered Stoic training can reduce broad FNE relative to an active control in college students and may increase the Stoic attitudes and behaviors the intervention is intended to cultivate.

These effects did not extend to significant between-condition improvements in broader measures of resilience, selfefficacy, or rumination, and reductions in FNE were not accompanied by attenuated subjective or cardiac responses to acute social evaluation.
Instead, Stoic training combined with immediate Negative Visualization was associated with greater cardiac mobilization during the TSST.

These divergent findings underscore the importance of distinguishing changes in relatively enduring cognitive vulnerabilities from immediate responses to acute stress and of considering the timing and context in which specific Stoic practices are applied.

Further research should determine which components of Stoic training drive reductions in FNE, establish whether these effects persist over time, and disentangle the cumulative effects of repeated Stoic practice from the acute effects of Negative Visualization.

If replicated and extended, these findings may establish a foundation for the further development of brief digital Stoic training as a scalable approach for targeting fear of negative evaluation in college populations, while also advancing a more nuanced understanding of how Stoic practices influence both enduring cognitive vulnerabilities and acute stress responding.
